title.narrative: IOM Migration, Business and Human Rights in Asia
IOM Migration, Business and Human Rights in Asia

description.narrative:
The main objective of the contribution is to promote full respect for the human and labour rights of migrant workers within supply chains in Asia. A specific focus is given to women and migrants in situations of vulnerability. Central to the rationale of the MBHR Asia programme are the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and their "Protect, Respect and Remedy" framework and the programme outcomes are structured along this framework.
PROTECT (Outcome 1): Improved labour migration governance that holds private sector actors accountable in protecting migrant workers' rights from a multi-sectoral, rights-based and gender-responsive approach. Output 1.1 Increased capacities and technical resources of national and subnational authorities and regional bodies in Asia in the design and implementation of policies related to labour migration governance, Responsible Business Conduct and the protection of migrant workers' rights in coordination with the private sector and the Civil Society Organisations Output 1.2 Increased availability of rights-based, gender-responsive and inclusive support and information services for migrant workers in coordination with Civil Society organizations, migrant networks and service providers.
RESPECT (Outcome 2): Improved corporate due diligence practices of private sector entities that respect the rights of migrant workers across their entire supply chains and at all stages of labour migration. Output 2.1 Improved knowledge and tools of private sector entities in the implementation of human rights due diligence and ethical recruitment and employment standards. Output 2.2 Increased opportunities for private sector stakeholders to engage in dialogues and collective actions around the responsible and transparent management of labour migration processes and the development of industry-led advocacy initiatives.
REMEDY (Outcome 3): Enhanced access for migrant workers to effective and gender-sensitive state justice and corporate grievance and remediation mechanisms. Output 3.1 Improved knowledge and tools of state actors and the private sector in the implementation of grievance mechanisms and the effective remediation of rights violations and abuses experienced by migrant workers. Output 3.2 Increased capacities and resources of civil society, migrant-driven organizations and trade unions in advancing migrant workers´ access to state-based justice and corporate grievance mechanisms.

Det övergripande målet för programmet är att främja full respekt för migrantarbetares mänskliga- och arbetsrättsliga rättigheter inom värdekedjor i Asien och fokuserar på viktiga regionala korridorer för arbetskraftsmigration, inklusive både ursprungs- och destinationsländer.
I enlighet med FNs vägledande principer för företagande och mänskliga rättigheter verkar insatsen för att säkra staters skyldighet att skydda (protect) migrantarbetares rättigheter, den privata sektorns ansvar att respektera och säkra (respect) migrantarbetares rättigheter i sina värdekedjor och rekryteringsprocesser, samt möjligheten till effektiva rättsmedel och kompensation för migrantarbetare vars rättigheter kränkts.
Länder som berörs av insatsen är Kambodja, Indonesien, Malaysia, Nepal, Filippinerna, Thailand och Vietnam. En regional komponent som involverar relevanta ASEAN-organ ingår också.

The overall objective of the programme is to promote full respect for the human and labour rights of migrant workers within supply chains in Asia. The contribution focuses on key regional labour migration corridors in Asia, including both countries of origin and destination.
In accordance with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the contribution works to secure the duty of states to protect the rights of migrant workers, the responsibility of the private sector to respect the rights of migrant workers in their value chains and recruitment processes, and the access to effective legal remedies and compensation for migrant workers whose rights have been violated.
Countries included in the programme are Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nepal, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. A regional component involving relevant ASEAN bodies is also included.

title.narrative: Decision on Contribution IOM Migration, Business and Human Rights in Asia

description.narrative:
Having now reached the mid-way point for implementation, the MBHR Asia programme is well underway to reaching it's intended outcomes. Promising results have appeard since implementation started in January 2024, allthough to a varying degree between the three pillars (outcome areas) of the program. Some examples of results include:
Policy level:
In 2025, Nepal formally adopted its Labour Migration Policy which integrates IOMs technical inputs. IOM contributed to the drafting or advancement of seven further national and regional policies or strategies, including Cambodias draft National Labour Migration Policy 20262035, Malaysias National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights 20252030, Indonesias renewed draft Presidential Regulation on Migrant Worker Protection Governance, and the Philippines draft Labour Migration Management Plan.
Corporate level:
The work relating to the private sector (oucome area 2 - "respect" pillar) continues to be a strong element in the programme and a major outcome of MBHR Asia has been improved private sector capacity and practice related to human rights due diligence (HRDD) and responsible recruitment. Since 2024, IOM has mobilized over USD 5 million in co-investment from 19 private sector partners, delivering tailored training, technical advisory, and tools that strengthened HRDD implementation across 1,089 entities at all levels of supply chains. The programme has driven concrete corporate policy changes. For example, a Swiss footwear company published its first global human rights policy; a Japanese electronics company revised its responsible recruitment policy for Malaysia; and a pharmaceutical corporation updated its global supplier guidance on responsible recruitment and recruitment fee repayment. Most critically, 7,270 migrant workers have seen direct improvements in their working conditions as a result of companies acting on IOM's findings and recommendations. In Thailand, four tire suppliers corrected employment practices for Cambodian migrant workers, issuing contracts, aligning wages with legal standards, and rectifying working hours, while the commissioning Japanese company subsequently rolled out ethical recruitment training across its own supplier network. A major food industry company implemented corrective action plans across seven Thai sugar suppliers, strengthening farmer awareness of worker rights and entitlements and building worker confidence to access grievance mechanisms without fear of retaliation. In Nepal, 717 workers secured employment in Saudi Arabia without being charged recruitment fees and related costs following an ethical recruitment pilot involving recruiters, brands, employers and government actors.
It is particularilty positive to note that the ambition to engage more with industry-wide coalitions and better include SMEs under the programme has progressed well. While bilateral engagements with large, multinational enterprises may be impactful through mobilization of funds and value chain outreach, these kinds of engagements tend to be time and resource consuming. Further strengthening the work with industry initiatives and SMEs (through employer organizations etc.)
Access to remedy:
Through IOMsupported civil society partners, 647 migrant workers and family members across Indonesia, Malaysia, Nepal, and Thailand have received legal aid and case management under the programmes Regional Remediation Fund, spanning cases of unpaid wages, recruitment fee overcharging, non-deployment, labour violations, and exploitation across fisheries, domestic work, transport, construction, and farming. These efforts resulted in USD 636,669 in remediation awards, with USD 335,249 already disbursed and went beyond financial recovery to empower affected workers as advocates within their own communities. A landmark case in Malaysia affirmed that migrant workers cannot be treated as a reserve labour pool, establishing a ruling that supports mandatory wage payment from the first day of arrival. Nonetheless, this area of work remains perhaps the most challenging one under the programme.
Throughout MBHR Asia, an integrated approach to democracy and human rights, gender equality, and environment and climate change has been applied. These priorities were embedded across governance reform, capacitybuilding, research, and private sector engagement. Gender-responsive provisions were integrated into three of the seven migration, business and human rights policies and strategies supported by IOM. Twelve of 22 human rights due diligence assessments conducted for companies operating in Asia produced gender-disaggregated insights or identified climate-related risks including heat exposure, gender-based violence, and pregnancy discrimination. Across countries, community-level campaigns integrated climate drivers of migration, floods, droughts, and livelihood disruption, into safe migration education.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
